The '''diamondback tritonia''' (''Tritonia festiva'') is a species of [[nudibranch]], a [[marine (ocean)|marine]] [[gastropod]] [[mollusk]] in the family [[Tritoniidae]].<ref>[https://www.seaslugforum.net/tritfest.htm Sea Slug Forum info]</ref> It is an opportunistic predator of other marine invertebrates.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://slugsite.us/bow/nudwk238.htm |title = Nudibranch of the Week isTritonia festiva}}</ref>

== Classification ==
The diamondback tritonia is classified within the Mollusca phylum, the Gastropoda class, the Nudibranchia order, the Tritotoniidae family, and the ''Tritonia'' genus. This species was first described as ''Lateribranchiaea festiva'' (Stearns, 1873).<ref>{{Cite web|title=WoRMS - World Register of Marine Species - Tritonia festiva (Stearns, 1873)|url=http://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxdetails&id=549413|access-date=2021-03-12|website=www.marinespecies.org}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
The diamondback tritonia inhabits the waters of the Pacific Ocean. Sightings have been most prevalent on the west coast of North America and have been reported as far north as Alaska.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tritonia festiva (Stearns, 1873)|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5190102|access-date=2021-03-12|website=www.gbif.org|language=en}}</ref> The species has also been identified along the coast of Japan and both North and South Korea.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Baba|first=Kikutaro|date=1969|title=Notes on the collection of Tritonia festiva (Stearns, 1873) from the seas of Japan (Gastropoda: Nudibranchia)|journal=Veliger|volume=12|issue=1|pages=132–134|via=eScholarship}}</ref>

== Habitat ==
The diamondback tritonia is a benthic organism as the sea floor is where this species finds its prey. Their flattened body plan allows for maneuverability into small spaces common in rocky intertidal areas.

== Body plan ==
[[File:Tritonia festiva, isla Santa Cruz 3.jpg|thumb|Intricate pattern along the back of a diamondback tritonia]]
The basic structure of all nudibranchs consists of a soft body that lacks a shell. Nudibranchs are [[Symmetry in biology|bilaterally symmetrical]] and oblong in shape as they are dorsoventrally flattened. However, from species to species, there is a great range of characteristics differentiating each species from one another.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brown|first=Eric|date=2011-04-29|title=Nudibranch Predators of Octocorallia|url=https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cnso_stucap/23|journal=HCNSO Student Capstones}}</ref> In the case of the diamondback tritonia, these nudibranchs are typically light pink, orange or white in color<ref>{{Cite web|title=Diamondback Tritonia (California Sea Slugs - Nudibranchs (and other marine Heterobranchia) of California) · iNaturalist|url=https://www.inaturalist.org/guide_taxa/2847|access-date=2021-04-06|website=iNaturalist|language=en}}</ref> and have an intricate pattern along their back. This pattern can vary amongst individuals.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tritonia Festiva|url=http://www.seaotter.com/marine/research/tritonia/festiva/html/festiva.jpg.html|access-date=2021-04-06|website=www.seaotter.com}}</ref> They also possess a vestigial girdle of chitinous ridges that separates them from other nudibranch species.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Description of the first tritoniid nudibranch found feeding on a zoanthid anthozoan, with a preliminary phylogeny of the Tritoniidae|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263090408|access-date=2021-04-06|website=ResearchGate|language=en}}</ref>

== Feeding ==
[[File:Tritonia_festiva,_isla_Santa_Cruz.jpg|thumb|Diamondback tritonia feeding on a sea whip]]
The diamondback tritonia preys on [[Octocorallia|soft corals]] including sea pens, sea pansies, and sea whips.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Katz|first=Paul|date=2007|title=Tritonia|journal=Scholarpedia|language=en|volume=2|issue=6|pages=3504|doi=10.4249/scholarpedia.3504|bibcode=2007SchpJ...2.3504K|issn=1941-6016|doi-access=free}}</ref> They feed on the young of these organisms as they are smaller and easier to consume.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Birkeland|first=Charles|date=1974|title=Interactions between a Sea Pen and Seven of Its Predators|journal=Ecological Monographs|volume=44|issue=2|pages=211–232|doi=10.2307/1942312|jstor=1942312|bibcode=1974EcoM...44..211B }}</ref> More specifically, the diamondback tritonia is the only known predator to the polyps of ''Discophyton rudyi,'' which are small, colony-forming soft corals found on the rocky shores of the Northeast Pacific Ocean.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goddard|first=Jeffrey H.R|date=2006-01-01|title=Stealthy slugs and communicating corals: polyp withdrawal by an aggregating soft coral in response to injured neighbors|url=http://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/10.1139/z05-178|journal=Canadian Journal of Zoology|language=en|volume=84|issue=1|pages=66–71|doi=10.1139/z05-178|s2cid=86206487 |issn=0008-4301|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Diamondback tritonias feed on these varying prey by using their digitate frontal veil to locate and attack them before the polyps can contract into a state of protection.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Goddard|first=J|date=2000|title=Tritonia festiva|url=https://www.seaslugforum.net/find/tritfest|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315070534/http://www.seaslugforum.net:80/find/tritfest |archive-date=2011-03-15 }}</ref>

== Reproduction and mating ==
This species is [[Hermaphrodite|simultaneously hermaphroditic]], meaning that they produce both eggs and sperm. Mating occurs as both individuals try to penetrate one another. The first to succeed is deemed the dominant male and the other individual deposits the fertilized eggs on a substratum to develop.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tritonia festiva, diamondback tritonia|url=https://www.sealifebase.se/summary/Tritonia-festiva.html|access-date=2021-04-06|website=www.sealifebase.se}}</ref>
